# National Veteran's Organization Donor Report

Prepare session

```{r}
remove(list = ls())
library(tidyverse)
donors <- read_csv("donors.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Initial Inspection

Familiarize

```{r}
# Inspect column names
col_names <- colnames(donors) |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  rename(Columns = "colnames(donors)") |> 
  arrange(Columns)
col_names

# Column types
col_types <- data.frame(
  col_name = names(donors),
  col_type = sapply(donors, class),
  row.names = NULL) |> 
  arrange(col_type)
col_types

# Summarise dataset
summary(donors)

# Inspect NAs
col_NA <- colSums(is.na(donors)) |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  rename(NA_Count = "colSums(is.na(donors))") |> 
  arrange(desc(NA_Count))
col_NA

total_donors <- nrow(donors)
col_NA_prop <- col_NA |> 
  mutate(NA_Prop = round(NA_Count / total_donors,2))
col_NA_prop
```

## Cleaning

Ensure clean character data

```{r}
# State data overview
summary(donors$state)
class(donors$state)

# State unique values
count_states <- length(unique(donors$state))
count_states # 57 tells us there is either misspelling, or non-domestic states

# Compare the state codes from the dataset with built-in R state codes
state_codes <- c(unique(donors$state))
non_state_terr <- c(setdiff(state_codes, state.abb))
non_state_terr

# Identify non-US-state territories
donors1 <- donors |> 
  mutate(
    isState = !(state %in% non_state_terr),
    .after = state) |> 
  mutate(state = as.factor(state))
class(donors1$state)

# Urbanicity data overview
summary(donors1$urbanicity)
class(donors1$urbanicity)

# Urbanicity unique values
unique(donors1$urbanicity)

# Convert urbanicity to factor
donors2 <- donors1 |>
  mutate(urbanicity = as.factor(urbanicity))
donors2

# Inspect gender
unique(donors2$gender)
class(donors2$gender)

# Convert gender to factor
donors3 <- donors2 |> 
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, levels = c("male", "female", "joint")))
donors3

# Inspect socio-economic status
summary(donors3$socioEconomicStatus)
unique(donors3$socioEconomicStatus)
class(donors3$socioEconomicStatus)

# Convert socioEconomicStatus to factor
donors_cl <- donors3 |> 
  mutate(socioEconomicStatus = as.factor(socioEconomicStatus))

donors_cl[c("state", "urbanicity", "socioEconomicStatus","gender")]

# Clear up space in memory
remove(donors, donors1, donors2, donors3)
```

## Major Aggregates and Visualizations

### Age

```{r}
# Donor age parameters
avg_age <- round(mean(donors_cl$age, na.rm = T),1)
med_age <- median(donors_cl$age, na.rm = T)
# Inner 90% of values
trim_avg_age <- round(mean(donors_cl$age, trim = 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

age_paras <- data.frame(
  metric = c('Mean', 'Trimmed Mean', 'Median'),
  value = c(avg_age, trim_avg_age, med_age))

age_paras

# Donor age visualization
donors_cl |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)

# Not super helpful, but getting practice with stripchart()
stripchart(
  donors_cl$age,
  method = "stack",
  pch = 16)

donors_cl |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) + 
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "#69b3a2",
    color = "#2c3e50",
    alpha = 0.7,
    outlier.color = "#e74c3c",
    outlier.shape = 21,
    outlier.fill = "#e74c3c",
    outlier.size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Donor Age",
    subtitle = "National Veteran's Organization Dataset",
    x = "Age (yrs)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()
  )
```

The histogram of donor age reveals a surprising pattern:

```{r}
# Even and odd age counts
even_odd_age <- data.frame(
  even = donors_cl |>
    filter(age %% 2 == 0) |> 
    nrow(),
  odd = donors_cl |>
    filter(age %% 2 == 1) |> 
    nrow(),
  na = donors_cl |>
    filter(is.na(age)) |> 
    nrow())
even_odd_age

# Difference between even aged donors and odd aged donors
even_odd_diff <- even_odd_age$even - even_odd_age$odd
even_odd_prop <- round(even_odd_diff / (even_odd_age$odd),2)
# even_odd_diff
# even_odd_prop
```

Out of 95,412 donors, there were 44,540 donors with an even number for age. There were 27,207 donors with an odd number and 23,665 without a collected value for age in the data set. It is my assumption that either an error during collection caused odd age values to be replaced with NA, or there is a systemic targeting of even-aged donors by the Veteran's Organization. Possibly an automated outreach that pings the donor every 2 years following an arbitrary, even-numbered age. Could use some further investigation.

### Urbanicity

This column categorizes the settlement type where a donor lives. Possible categories are city, rural, suburb, town, and urban.

```{r}
# Donor settlement categories
urbcit_props <- data.frame(prop.table(table(donors_cl$urbanicity)))
urbcit_props
barplot(
  table(donors_cl$urbanicity),
  main = "Why the relative scarcity of urban donors?",
  las = 1,
  ylab = "Count",
  cex.axis = 0.75,
  col = c(rep("gray",4), "red"))
```

Quick multi-factor analyses

```{r}
# Donor home settlement type and mailing response
urbCit_respMail <- round(proportions(table(donors_cl$respondedMailing, donors_cl$urbanicity)),3)
barplot(urbCit_respMail)

# Donor home settlement type and gender
gend_urbCit <- round(proportions(table(donors_cl$gender, donors_cl$urbanicity)),3)
# Plot theme
gender_colors <- c("#4575b4", "#d73027", "#fee090")

barplot(
  gend_urbCit,
  beside = TRUE,
  legend.text = TRUE,
  main = "Females dominated donations across the whole dataset",
  xlab = "Settlement Type",
  ylab = "Proportion of all donors with non-NA genders",
  col = gender_colors,
  border = "white")
```

### Time Since First and Last Donation

```{r}
# Calculating frequencies "the hard way"
since_first_prop <- data.frame(
  prop.table(table(donors_cl$yearsSinceFirstDonation)))

since_first_prop |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Var1, y = Freq)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

# Plotting frequencies without calculation
donors_cl |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = yearsSinceFirstDonation)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "identity")

# Using position = "fill" to investigate response to mailing versus time since last gift - pretty useless
donors_cl |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = monthsSinceLastDonation, fill = respondedMailing)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill")
```

## Percentile Experimentation

### Total Donation Amount

The "zero-th" percentile gives the minimum value, 50th gives the median, and 100th gives the maximum.

```{r}
# First quartile
quantile(donors_cl$totalGivingAmount, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
# Third quartile
quantile(donors_cl$totalGivingAmount, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
# All at once
quantile(donors_cl$totalGivingAmount, probs = seq(0, 1.0, by = 0.1), na.rm = TRUE)
```

###  Number of Donations

```{r}
quantile(donors_cl$numberGifts, probs = seq(0,1,by=0.25))
```

### First and Last Donation Info

```{r}
# Time since first donation (years)
quantile(donors_cl$yearsSinceFirstDonation, probs = seq(0,1,by=0.25), na.rm = TRUE)

# Time since most recent donation (months)
quantile(donors_cl$monthsSinceLastDonation, probs = seq(0,1,by=0.25), na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Two Variable Analysis

### Grouped Donation Totals

Data with many outliers can cause issues when represented by box plots. Either a different visual representation should be chosen, or outliers should be removed. By omitting the outliers, we discover that the distribution of total giving amount is not correlated to home settlement type.

```{r}
# Total donation vs home settlement type
boxplot(data = donors_cl, totalGivingAmount ~ urbanicity)

# Total donation vs home settlement type, omitting outliers
boxplot(data = donors_cl, totalGivingAmount ~ urbanicity, outline = FALSE)
```

The median time since last donation seems to be independent of whether the donor responded to the mailing. The distribution of the number of gifts, grouped by response to the mailing, seems to show a relationship that can be investigated further.

```{r}
boxplot(data = donors_cl, monthsSinceLastDonation ~ respondedMailing)
boxplot(data = donors_cl, numberGifts ~ respondedMailing, outline = FALSE)
```

## Measures of Variability

### Range

The range of the number of children registered to each donor is 6. It is important to note that this category is 87% NA, so any conclusions about the donor data set as a whole may be difficult to trust.

```{r}
range_children <- max(donors_cl$numberChildren, na.rm = TRUE) - min(donors_cl$numberChildren, na.rm = TRUE)
range_children
```

Another way of calculating range using the average gift amount

```{r}
range_avg_don <- round(diff(range(donors_cl$averageGiftAmount)),2)
range_avg_don
```

### Interquartile Range

The interquartile range is more resistant to outliers than a pure range calculation. If average donation were uniformly distributed, it would be expected that the IQR would be half the range. However, outliers in this data set cause the IQR to be much tighter than that.

```{r}
# quantile(donors_cl$averageGiftAmount, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
# quantile(donors_cl$averageGiftAmount, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR_avg_don <- diff(quantile(donors_cl$averageGiftAmount, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE))
IQR_avg_don
```

IQR using R's built-in function:

```{r}
IQR_func_avg_don <- IQR(donors_cl$averageGiftAmount, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR_func_avg_don
```
